Let’s break this down.  

The premise says:  
> Nobody is neither an owner of a The Body Shop soap nor a frequent consumer of Lush soap.  

In logical terms:  
Let \( A \) = "owner of a The Body Shop soap"  
Let \( B \) = "frequent consumer of Lush soap"  

"Neither A nor B" means \(\neg A \land \neg B\).  
"Nobody is neither A nor B" means \(\neg \exists x (\neg A(x) \land \neg B(x))\), which is equivalent to \(\forall x (A(x) \lor B(x))\).  

So the premise says: Everyone is either an owner of a The Body Shop soap or a frequent consumer of Lush soap (or both).  

The conclusion says:  
> Nobody is neither a frequent consumer of Lush soap nor an owner of a The Body Shop soap.  

"Neither B nor A" means \(\neg B \land \neg A\), which is the same as \(\neg A \land \neg B\).  
So the conclusion says the same thing as the premise: \(\forall x (A(x) \lor B(x))\).  

Since the premise and conclusion are logically equivalent, the argument is deductively valid.  

Final answer: valid
